blogs/building-a-cross-cloud-data-pipeli.title: Building a Cross-Cloud Data Pipeline
blogs/building-a-cross-cloud-data-pipeli.description:
Date: 2024-10-27 Tags: Data Engineering, Google Cloud Platform, Amazon Web Services, BigQuery, S3|>cloud(5)|> |<description BCCDP|<
Modern data stacks often span multiple clouds due to acquisitions, best-of-breed services, or cost optimization. This exercise explores querying data stored in AWS S3 directly from Google BigQuery using BigQuery's external table functionality, eliminating the need for complex ETL and data duplication. Setting up a secure, read-only connection from GCP to AWS. Configuring IAM roles and permissions on both platforms. Creating and querying a BigQuery external table over S3 data. Observations on performance and cost implications. GCP Project: analytics-prod-001 AWS Account: data-lake-account Key Services: GCP BigQuery & IAM, AWS S3 & IAM. Data: Sample CSV files (~2 GB) in an S3 bucket: s3://company-raw-data/logs/. Admin access to both GCP and AWS accounts. A GCP service account created specifically for this integration. S3 bucket with sample data already in place. GCP Side: Created a service account (bq-s3-reader@) and generated a JSON key. AWS Side: Created an IAM user, attached a custom policy granting s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket on the specific bucket. Associated the GCP service account's key with this user. BigQuery: Used the Cloud Console to create an external data source, providing the AWS user's access key and secret. SQL Execution: Wrote a CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE DDL statement pointing to the S3 URI and defining the CSV schema. Challenge: Initial "Access Denied" errors from BigQuery. Fix: Realized the AWS IAM policy needed an explicit "s3:ListBucket" action on the bucket resource (not just the objects). Updated the policy, and the table creation succeeded. Challenge: CSV file had a malformed row. Fix: Used the MAX_BAD_RECORDS option in the external table definition to skip errors, but noted this for data quality review. The setup is surprisingly straightforward for read-only, ad-hoc querying. The data never moves to GCP; BigQuery orchestrates the compute and pulls only the necessary data from S3. Performance: Querying is noticeably slower than native BigQuery tables, especially for complex JOIN operations. This is expected as it's scanning data over the internet. Cost Model: You pay for BigQuery compute (bytes processed) + AWS S3 GET requests and data transfer out. For infrequent queries on cold data, this can be cheaper than replicating the entire dataset. For production, consider using AWS Role-based access (instead of user keys) for better security, though it requires a more complex "GCP Workload Identity Federation" setup. For frequently queried data, set up a scheduled materialized view inside BigQuery to cache results and improve performance. Test with columnar formats like Parquet or ORC for significantly better query performance and cost efficiency. BigQuery's federated query capability is a powerful tool for a multi-cloud strategy, enabling a single point of analysis. The key takeaway is the trade-off: unparalleled flexibility vs. query performance. It's perfect for exploratory analysis on raw data in S3 before committing to a full migration or ETL process.

blogs/powershell-onboarding-scripts-in-a.title: PowerShell Onboarding Scripts in a Hybrid AD-Azure Environment
blogs/powershell-onboarding-scripts-in-a.description:
Date: 2024-10-27 Tags: IT Support, Automation, Active Directory, PowerShell, Azure AD, Onboarding|>it-support(5)|> |<description POSHADAE|< Manual onboarding for new hires (creating AD accounts, assigning licenses, setting up home drives) was error-prone and took ~45 minutes per user. Developed a PowerShell script to automate 90% of the process, ensuring consistency and freeing up L2/L3 time for more complex tasks. The logic and structure of the main automation script. Integration with on-prem Active Directory and Azure AD Connect. Error handling and logging for support team visibility. Domain Controller: Windows Server 2019 (On-prem) Sync Tool: Azure AD Connect (v2.x) Client: Administrative workstation with RSAT and AzureAD module. Script Location: \\fileserver\IT\Scripts\Automation\Onboarding
Pre-populated CSV template from HR (newhires_YYYYMMDD.csv) in a secure share. Pre-defined AD security groups (Staff-Office, Staff-Remote, Department-*). Available Microsoft 365 licenses in the tenant. Script Trigger: Manual run from secure IT workstation after HR notification. .\Start-NewHireOnboarding.ps1 -CsvPath "\\hrserver\secure\newhires_20241027.csv" Core Script Logic (Abridged): # 1. Import CSV and validate data $NewHires = Import-Csv $CsvPath foreach ($User in $NewHires) { # 2. Generate username (first.last) and check for duplicates $SamAccountName = "$($User.FirstName).$($User.LastName)".ToLower() # 3. Create AD User Account $Password = ConvertTo-SecureString -String (New-ComplexPassword) -AsPlainText -Force New-ADUser -Name "$($User.FirstName) $($User.LastName)" ` -SamAccountName $SamAccountName ` -UserPrincipalName "$SamAccountName@corp.example.com" ` -AccountPassword $Password ` -Enabled $true ` -Path "OU=Users,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com" ` -OtherAttributes @{title=$User.JobTitle; department=$User.Department} # 4. Add to Security Groups based on Department/Location Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "Department-$($User.Department)" -Members $SamAccountName Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "Location-$($User.Location)" -Members $SamAccountName # 5. Create Home Drive and set permissions $HomeDrivePath = "\\fileserver\homes\$SamAccountName" New-Item -Path $HomeDrivePath -ItemType Directory icacls $HomeDrivePath /grant "$($env:USERDOMAIN)\$SamAccountName`:(OI)(CI)F" # 6. Wait for AD Connect sync, then assign M365 license Start-Sleep -Seconds 180 Connect-AzureAD $License = Get-AzureADSubscribedSku | Where-Object {$_.SkuPartNumber -eq "ENTERPRISEPACK"} Set-AzureADUserLicense -ObjectId "$SamAccountName@corp.example.com" ` -AssignedLicenses @{SkuId = $License.SkuId} # 7. Log all actions Write-Log -Message "Created user: $SamAccountName" -Level INFO } Challenge: Azure AD Connect sync delay caused "user not found" errors when trying to assign licenses immediately. # ERROR: Set-AzureADUserLicense : Error occurred while executing SetUserLicenses # Code: Request_ResourceNotFound Fix: Added a Start-Sleep -Seconds 180 wait and implemented a retry loop that checks Azure AD for user existence before proceeding. $RetryCount = 0 do { Start-Sleep -Seconds 30 $AzureUser = Get-AzureADUser -Filter "userPrincipalName eq '$UPN'" $RetryCount++ } while ($null -eq $AzureUser -and $RetryCount -lt 10) Challenge: HR CSV sometimes had missing department data. Fix: Added validation logic that sends an alert to the IT ticket system and skips that user, rather than failing the entire batch. if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($User.Department)) { Write-Log -Message "Missing department for $($User.Email). Creating ticket." -Level WARN New-ServiceNowTicket -ShortDescription "Onboarding Data Issue" -Description "User missing department" continue } Time Saved: Reduced manual work from 45 to ~5 minutes (just verification). Batch of 10 users now takes 20 minutes instead of 7.5 hours. Error Reduction: Zero typos in usernames or group assignments since implementation. Unexpected Benefit: The detailed log file (Onboarding_20241027.log) became invaluable for auditing and proving compliance during internal audits. Integrate with HR System: Next phase is to call the HRIS API directly instead of using CSV files. Self-Service Portal: Build a web front-end where managers can trigger onboarding for contractors with pre-approved templates. Offboarding Script: Build the counterpart script that disables accounts, archives data, and reclaims licenses with the same rigor. Automation in IT support isn't about replacing people; it's about eliminating repetitive, low-value tasks that are prone to human error. This script paid for itself in time savings within the first month of use and significantly improved the new hire experience (everything was ready at 9 AM on day one). The key to success was robust error handling and comprehensive logging—the script needed to fail gracefully and tell us exactly why.

blogs/secret-management-in-aws-secrets-m.title: Secret Management in AWS Secrets Manager vs. Google Secret Manager
blogs/secret-management-in-aws-secrets-m.description: Date: 2024-10-27 Tags: Security, DevOps, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud Platform, Secrets Management |>it-support(5) cloud(5)|> |<description SMASMGPSM|< Managing application secrets (API keys, passwords, certificates) is a fundamental security requirement. This post compares the core features, pricing, and developer experience of the two leading cloud-native secret managers. A practical comparison of core operations: creating, accessing, rotating, and auditing secrets. Analysis of integration patterns with their respective ecosystems (Lambda vs. Cloud Functions, ECS vs. GKE). Simple cost estimation for a typical microservices workload. Tools: AWS CLI, Google Cloud SDK, Python boto3 & google-cloud-secret-manager libraries. Test Setup: One secret ("database-password") created in both services. A simple Python script to retrieve and use the secret. Created a secret with a key-value pair in both consoles and via CLI. Wrote identical Python functions to retrieve the latest secret version from each manager. Examined built-in rotation features and audit logs (CloudTrail vs. Cloud Audit Logs). Reviewed IAM/Resource Manager policies for fine-grained access control. Challenge: GCP's Secret Manager uses the concept of secret versions more explicitly. Accessing the secret payload requires specifying the version path (e.g., latest). Insight: This is not a challenge but a design difference. AWS returns the latest by default in its primary API call, but versions are still maintained. Fix: For GCP, ensured my client code always accessed "latest" for the default use case. Feature Parity: Both are robust, offering automatic rotation (with integration for RDS/Aurora or Cloud SQL), fine-grained access policies, and mandatory audit logging. Developer Experience: AWS feels more integrated with its own ecosystem (e.g., direct reference in RDS, Lambda environment variables). GCP's versioning is more explicit and feels integrated with its CI/CD and infrastructure-as-code tools (Terraform, Deployment Manager). Pricing: GCP charges per secret version (active and archived), while AWS charges per secret and per API call. For secrets that change often, GCP's model can become more expensive if old versions aren't cleaned up. For Multi-Cloud: Consider a third-party tool like HashiCorp Vault for a unified interface, accepting the operational overhead. Cost Optimization: Implement a lifecycle policy to automatically delete old secret versions after a set period (e.g., 30 days). Next step: Test the client-side caching libraries offered by both to reduce API calls, latency, and cost. You cannot go wrong with either service for cloud-native projects. The choice often boils down to which cloud you are primarily in. The main differentiators are the pricing model and the degree of ecosystem integration. If your team is already invested in one cloud, using its native secret manager will provide the smoothest experience. The exercise solidified that the most important factor is using a dedicated secrets manager—not which one you choose.

blogs/troubleshooting-gpo-driven-drive-m.title: Troubleshooting GPO-Driven Drive Mappings
blogs/troubleshooting-gpo-driven-drive-m.description: Date: 2024-10-27 Tags: IT Support, Troubleshooting, Group Policy, Windows, Networking, DFS|>it-support(5)|> |<description TGDD|< Sudden flood of tickets from the Finance department: "Network drives missing!" "Can't access shared folders!" Initial symptoms pointed to a widespread Group Policy failure affecting drive mappings for an entire OU. The systematic troubleshooting methodology from client to server. Discovery of an unexpected dependency between print and file services. The fix and long-term solution implemented. Environment: Clients: Windows 10 22H2 (Finance OU) Domain Controllers: 2x Server 2019 File Server: Server 2019 (FS01) hosting DFS Namespace Print Server: Same physical server as FS01 (different instance) Tools: gpresult, rsop.msi, Event Viewer, PowerShell Standard drive mappings deployed via Group Policy Preferences (GPP) with Item-level targeting (Finance department security group). DFS Namespace: \\corp.example.com\Shares\Finance Initial Triage on Client: # 1. Check basic connectivity ping fs01.corp.example.com # OK # 2. Check if policy is applying gpresult /h gp_report.html # Finding: "Finance Drives" GPO shows as "Applied" # But drives F: and G: are not present in Explorer. # 3. Force policy update and check logs gpupdate /force Get-WinEvent -LogName "Application" -Source "GroupPolicy*" -MaxEvents 20 | Format-List Found critical error:Event ID 4098: The processing of Group Policy failed. Windows attempted to read the file \\corp.example.com\SysVol\corp.example.com\Policies\{GUID}\Machine\Preferences\Drives\Drives.xml and failed. The error was: The network path was not found. Server-Side Investigation: # 1. Check SYSVOL replication and accessibility Test-Path "\\corp.example.com\SysVol" # OK # 2. Check the specific GPO's files $GPOPath = "\\corp.example.com\SysVol\corp.example.com\Policies\{GUID}\Machine\Preferences\Drives\Drives.xml" Test-Path $GPOPath # FALSE - File is missing! # 3. Check DFS Health Get-DfsrState -ComputerName DC01 -Verbose # All replication groups show "Normal" Challenge: The Drives.xml file existed on DC02 but not on DC01. Why wasn't DFSR replicating it? Breakthrough Discovery: Checking the file server's event logs revealed the root cause. Get-WinEvent -ComputerName FS01 -LogName "System" -MaxEvents 50 | Where-Object {$_.Id -eq 2013} Critical Event Found:Source: srv Event ID: 2013 The server was unable to allocate from the system nonpaged pool because the pool was empty. The Print Spooler service on FS01 had a memory leak and consumed all non-paged pool memory, which also killed the Server service (LanmanServer). No Server service = no SYSVOL access = failed GPO processing. Immediate Fix: # On FS01 (via emergency RDP): Stop-Service Spooler Start-Service Spooler Restart-Service LanmanServer # Force AD replication of the missing GPO file from DC02 to DC01 repadmin /syncall DC01 /AdeP Client drives reappeared after the next gpupdate /force. The Hidden Dependency: We had no idea that a runaway print spooler on a file/print server could break Group Policy processing for drive mappings. The three services seemed unrelated but shared the same kernel resource (non-paged pool). Scope Creep: What started as a "missing drives" ticket for Finance turned into a critical infrastructure issue affecting anyone whose primary Domain Controller was DC01. Lesson: Always check system resource exhaustion (memory, handles, pool) on servers when seeing "network path not found" errors that aren't actually network-related. Short-term: Implement a monitoring alert for "Server Event ID 2013" on all Windows servers. Medium-term: Migrate the print spooler service to a dedicated, isolated server instance. Long-term: Review all GPOs. Consider migrating drive maps from GPP (which relies on client-side XML file access) to logon scripts or PowerShell that are more resilient to temporary file server issues. This incident reinforced classic troubleshooting hierarchy: always start at the physical/network layer, then move up. We initially overthought the GPO logic when the problem was a resource starvation on a server. The most valuable tool was cross-referencing client errors with server logs. The Event ID 4098 on the client pointed to the file, but the Event ID 2013 on the server revealed the true cause. Documenting this chain has been added to our L2 Knowledge Base under "Unexpected GPO Failures" with the key insight: When drives disappear, check the print server.

blogs/weaponizing-public-buckets.html.title: Weaponizing Public Buckets
blogs/weaponizing-public-buckets.html.description: Date: 2024-10-27 Tags: Penetration Testing, Cloud Security, Amazon Web Services, Reconnaissance, Privilege Escalation|>cybersecurity(5)|> |<description WPB|< During an external penetration test, misconfigured cloud storage is a frequent and high-impact finding. This entry documents a real-world attack chain: discovering a public AWS S3 bucket, analyzing its contents, and leveraging found credentials to pivot into the cloud environment. The reconnaissance phase using automated and manual tools. Analyzing exfiltrated data for secrets. Demonstrating a privilege escalation path from stolen IAM credentials. Attacker Machine (Kali Linux): └── Tools: `s3scanner`, `awscli`, `bucket-stream`, `truffleHog`, `PACU` Target Scope: *.examplecorp.com (Bug Bounty Program) Valid AWS account (for CLI profile configuration). Tools installed and configured. Legal authorization to test the target (via Bug Bounty program scope). Enumeration: Used s3scanner with a custom wordlist based on target names. python3 s3scanner.py --bucket-wordlist targets.txt --out-file buckets.txt Found: dev-app-backups.examplecorp.com. Inspection: The bucket had List and Get permissions for "Any Authenticated AWS User." aws s3 ls s3://dev-app-backups.examplecorp.com --no-sign-request # Found: `application.tar.gz`, `config-backup.zip` Exfiltration & Analysis: Downloaded the config-backup.zip file. It contained a .env file with what appeared to be AWS keys. # Quick Python check for key format import re with open('.env', 'r') as f: if re.search(r'AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}', f.read()): print("[!] Potential AWS Access Key Found!") Challenge: The stolen keys (AKIA...) were inactive in the us-east-1 region. Fix: Used the AWS CLI's --region flag to enumerate all commercial regions. The keys were active in ap-southeast-2. for region in $(aws ec2 describe-regions --query 'Regions[].RegionName' --output text); do AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$STOLEN_KEY AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$STOLEN_SECRET \ aws sts get-caller-identity --region $region 2>/dev/null && echo "[+] Active in: $region" done The Pivot: The compromised IAM user (backup-bot) had the managed policy AmazonS3FullAccess. This allowed us to write a malicious Lambda function and trigger it, effectively moving from storage to compute. Unexpected Finding: The .env file also contained a hashed password for an internal Jenkins server, which reused the same secret. The Real Impact: This wasn't just data exposure. It was a foothold. The chain was: Public Bucket → Stolen Keys → Assume Role (via attached policy) → Lateral Movement. For Defense: Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level. Use IAM policies, not bucket policies, for granular control. Rotate credentials before storing them in backups. For Offense: Next steps would involve using the compromised role to enumerate IAM policies, check for SSM parameters, and attempt to launch EC2 instances for a persistent reverse shell. Misconfigured storage is rarely an isolated finding. It's a critical node in a potential attack graph. The exercise reinforced the principle of "assume breach." Even low-privilege, non-human credentials found in backups must be treated as catastrophic leaks, as they often have attached permissions or lead to other systems. EOL

projects/turning-32-bit-laptop-into-an-n.title: Turning 32-bit laptop into an nftables Firewall
projects/turning-32-bit-laptop-into-an-n.description:
Date: Jun 14, 2026 Tags: Network Security Firewall Log Management Linux nftables rsyslog|>cybersecurity(9) it-support(8)|> |<This project repurposed a retired 32-bit laptop into a Linux-based firewall for a small cybersecurity lab. Using AntiX Linux, nftables, dnsmasq, rsyslog, and logrotate, the firewall provides network address translation (NAT), stateful packet filtering, DNS sinkholing, and centralized logging.|<Project Summary This project repurposed a retired 32-bit laptop into a Linux-based firewall for a small cybersecurity lab. Using AntiX Linux, nftables, dnsmasq, rsyslog, and logrotate, the firewall provides network address translation (NAT), stateful packet filtering, DNS sinkholing, and centralized logging. The implementation was validated through connectivity, domain-blocking, and traffic-filtering tests while addressing challenges associated with aging hardware and limited resources.
Firewall is one of the most common and crucial defenses for network security. It controls incoming and outgoing traffic based on predefined rules. Due to limited resources, I am using an old laptop running on 32-bit AntiX Linux. The firewall will use the nftables, the default backend firewall of Linux. Configure network configuration for the AntiX Linux. Configure AntiX Linux as a nftables firewall and DNS sinkhole. Configure Log rotation. Configure Lab Router for the lab. Apply, test, and verify basic firewall rules. Figure 1 shows the network diagram for this entry. The firewall will use nftables for Network Address Translation and filtering on the network and transport layer. While dnsmasq is used for DNS sinkholing in the application layer. The Lab router will bridge the lab hosts to external networks.
Figure 1: Network diagramSoftware and Hardware components used: Installed AntiX Linux with atleast 2 Network Interface Cards (NIC). SSH enabled on AntiX for remote management. I start by renaming the laptop's interfaces. Rationale By setting the interface names to something more intuitive like lan0 and wan0, it will be easier for the future to manage, test, and troubleshooting in the future.
Renaming wan0 and lan0 interface I first identified the MAC Addresses of the interface with ip addr, then changed their NAME= on /etc/udev/rules.d/70-persistent-net.rules. Then, I configured the network interfaces. To make IP addresses easier to distinguish, and given that wan0 is on 192.168.11.0/24. I set lan0 interface to 173.16.0.0/24 and intended to use 10.0.0.0/24 for the lab. Figure 2 shows the current network connection on the firewall host. Network interface configuration In line 12-15, I set the lan0 to 172.168.0.1/24, it is important that the interface connected to this is also on the same network. In line 18-27, wan0 I set the static IP address of the firewall host to 192.168.11.200, setting static IP on servers and network hosts helps with accessibility and reduce configuration errors. In line 30, I added a route to LabNetwork (10.0.0.0/24) via firwall's lan0 (172.16.0.1) interface was specified. Without this, traffic going to 10.0.0.0/24 will be forwarded to 192.168.11.1 (gateway). ... 7 8 auto lo 9 iface lo inet loopback 10 11 # LAN - (Ethernet) 12 auto lan0 13 iface lan0 inet static 14 address 172.16.0.1 15 netmask 255.255.255.0 16 17 # WAN (Wireless) 18 auto wan0 19 iface wan0 inet static 20 address 192.168.11.200 21 netmask 255.255.255.0 22 gateway 192.168.11.1 23 dns-nameservers 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4 24 25 26 27 wpa-conf /etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant.conf 28 29 # Route to LAB network 30 up ip route add 10.0.0.0/24 via 172.16.0.2 dev lan0
Figure 2: Network connection and routing table on firewall host (AntiX Linux). I enabled IP forwarding and Network Address Translation (NAT) on the firewall. Rationale The default policy on all chains for table inet filter was set to drop following a Zero Trust approach where all connections are denied unless explicitly allowed. Initial nftables firewall config The logging prefix on my config will follow the pattern NFT-[CHAIN]-[ACTION]-[KEYWORD] to make logs easier to analyze and because the action is not included on nftables logs by default. 1 flush ruleset 2 3 table inet filter { 4 chain input { 5 type filter hook input priority filter; policy drop; 6 iif "lo" accept 7 ct state established,related accept 8 ct state invalid log prefix "NFT-IN-DROP-INVALID " drop 9 ip saddr 10.0.0.50 tcp dport 22 accept 10 tcp dport 53 accept 11 udp dport 53 accept 12 icmp type { echo-reply, echo-request } accept 13 log prefix "NFT-IN-DROP-DEFAULT " 14 } 15 16 chain forward { 17 type filter hook forward priority filter; policy drop; 18 ct state established,related accept 19 ct state invalid log prefix "NFT-FOR-DROP-INVALID " drop 20 ip daddr 9.9.9.9 log prefix "NFT-FOR-DROP-QUAD9 " drop 21 tcp dport { 80, 443 } accept 22 udp dport { 53, 123 } accept 23 icmp type { echo-reply, echo-request } accept 24 log prefix "NFT-FOR-DROP-DEFAULT " 25 } 26 27 chain output { 28 type filter hook output priority filter; policy drop; 29 ct state established,related accept 30 ct state invalid log prefix "NFT-OUT-DROP-INVALID " drop 31 hour "17:00"-"04:00" tcp dport { 80, 443, 53 } log prefix "NFT-OUT-ACCEPT-OFFHOUR_TRAFFIC " accept 32 hour "17:00"-"04:00" udp dport { 53, 123 } log prefix "NFT-OUT-ACCEPT-OFFHOUR_TRAFFIC " accept 33 tcp dport { 53, 80, 443 } accept 34 udp dport { 53, 123 } accept 35 icmp type { echo-reply, echo-request } accept 36 log prefix "NFT-OUT-DROP-DEFAULT " 37 } 38 } 39 table ip nat { 40 chain prerouting { 41 type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat; policy accept; 42 iifname "lan0" udp dport 53 dnat to 172.16.0.1 43 iifname "lan0" tcp dport 53 dnat to 172.16.0.1 44 } 45 46 chain postrouting { 47 type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept; 48 oifname "wan0" masquerade 49 } 50 } Since nftables is filtering on the OSI network layer (L3) and transport layer (L4). I also added a DNS Sinkhole using dnsmasq to filter domains. In Figure 7, I blocked the domain chess.com for testing purposes. 1 # DNS sinkhole list 2 address=/chess.com/ Figure 3: List of domain names blocked on /etc/dnsmasq.d/blocklist.conf. Lastly, I set up the logging mechanism on rsyslog using the config on Figure 4. This creates dedicated log files to store firewall logs. The $syslogtag was set by using imfile on rsyslog.conf. 1 # 1. Capture Firewall logs 2 :msg, contains, "NFT-" /var/log/nftables.log 3 & stop 4 5 # 2. Capture DNS queries 6 if ($syslogtag == 'dnsmasq_log') then { 7 /var/log/dns.log 8 stop 9 } 10 Figure 4: 1. All logs that has string that has "NFT-" will be stored on /var/log/nftables.log. 2. All dnsmasq_log will be stored on /var/log/dns.logImporting imfile module on rsyslog.conf This gives rsyslog access to dnsmasq.log to add tag=dnsmasq_log # <Redacted> 23 module(load="imfile") 24 25 input(type="imfile" 26 File="/var/log/dnsmasq.log" 27 Tag="dnsmasq_log" 28 Severity="info" 29 Facility="local0") # <Redacted> I created a logrotate config that keeps logs in manageable size. Since dns.log would certainly contain a lot more logs, I set the frequency to daily and only store up to 7 log archives at once.
Figure 5 Log rotation config on /etc/logrotate.d/firewall. I set the network configuration first by following Figure 6 and Figure 7. Figure 6: Lab router's WAN configuration. Figure 7: Lab router's LAN configuration. Then, I disabled Network Address Translation (NAT) on the lab router. Architecture The router will now forward traffic to its default gateway (firewall's lan0 interface) without changing the source IP addresses. With the placement of the firewall, disabling NAT on the edge router allows the firewall to see internal IP addresses which gives more control and insights over the traffic coming in and out of the lab.
Figure 8: NAT was disabled on the lab router. I applied the nftables rules and for the dnsmasq using the command below. sudo nft -f /etc/nftables.conf sudo service dnsmasq restart sudo service rsyslog restart Figure 9: Apply the nftables.conf rules and restart dnsmasq and rsyslog service. I connected to the LabNetwork and tested the created rules. Based on the test summary (see Figure 10), the nftables and dnsmasq implementation is working as expected. Figure 10. In order to properly parse them on the SIEM, I need to use different decoders. nftables is mainly for filtering Layer 3 (Network) and Layer 4 (Transport) traffic. It can also act as a stateful firewall. For blocking domains, using IP ranges could potentially cause inconvenience and holes on the network. Many modern websites are being delivered or tunneled via the massive IP blocks of companies like Cloudflare. DNS Sinkholing solves this specific problem. Devices generate a lot of DNS query. While it might be useful to log for correlation and attack mapping, it will also be accompanied with a lot of noise. I tried triggering a firewall drop rule and the log shows it was triggered on a different time. The longer the inaccuracy on the time, the more it would be confusing to correlate them especially across multiple hosts. This shows the importance of synchronized time across systems. Setup Wazuh server for centralized log collection and to monitor lab hosts. Update firewall rules for better security. Setup windows server and vulnerable hosts inside the lab. Attack the vulnerable hosts inside the lab This project successfully turned and old 32-bit laptop into a functioning firewall for my simple cybersecurity lab. It provided network address translation, network and transport layer filtering, along with stateful filtering using nftables. It also functions as dns sinkhole for blocking domains using dnsmasq. Logs are recorded on the firewall for log correlation and analysis. The logs are also rotated to prevent storage issues.While working in this project, I realized the limitations of L3/L4 firewalls in network security. That's why I added domain sinkholing on the go to try and imitate the basic network security capabilites most real world corporate network have. I also learned the critical value of syncing time across systems as it is one of the fields used for correlation.In the next entries, I would setup a Wazuh server that will store logs of lab hosts. Having a centralized place to view and correlate logs would make it easier to discover anomalies on the network. I will also install and attack a windows server and vulnerable hosts in the lab.

tags/log-management.html.title: Log Management
tags/log-management.html.description: Log Management is the systemic approach to generating, transmitting, aggregating, analyzing, and archiving telemetry data across an infrastructure. In a security and operations context, it establishes the fundamental baseline of visibility required to monitor system health, verify policy enforcement, detect anomalous behavior, and maintain a forensic audit trail of network events. Log Generation & Instrumentation The process where operating systems, applications, and security appliances record discrete events (such as kernel drops, authentication failures, or service restarts) to local storage files like /var/log/syslog. Log Aggregation & Transport Shipping local telemetry data across a network to a centralized repository using standard logging protocols (such as syslog or encrypted transport agents), ensuring logs are preserved even if the generating endpoint is compromised. Log Rotation & Lifecycle Management Automating storage maintenance by systematically compressing, archiving, or purging old log files (utilizing utilities like logrotate) to ensure continuous system availability and prevent disk-space exhaustion. Parsing & Normalization Transforming unstructured, raw text logs into structured fields (like JSON or key-value pairs), making it possible to query, index, and correlate data efficiently in upstream analytics platforms. Operational Troubleshooting: Enables IT support and systems engineers to diagnose application crashes, hardware faults, and configuration errors by analyzing historical system state transitions. Firewall Rule Validation: Provides real-time feedback loops during security engineering tasks, confirming whether stateful rulesets (like nftables chains) are successfully matching, logging, and dropping unauthorized traffic. SIEM Ingestion Readiness: Acts as the essential plumbing layer that prepares unstructured infrastructure data for ingestion into Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems for behavioral alerting. tags/nftables.html.title: nftables
tags/nftables.html.description: nftables is the modern Linux kernel packet classification framework designed to replace the legacy iptables, ip6tables, arptables, and ebtables infrastructure. It provides high-performance firewalling, Network Address Translation (NAT), and packet mangling by utilizing a compact pseudo-virtual machine inside the Linux kernel to execute classification rules efficiently. Tables: The top-level containers that hold chains. Unlike iptables, there are no built-in tables; they are explicitly defined by the user and tied to specific protocol families (e.g., ip, ip6, inet, bridge). Chains: Containers for rules that hook directly into the Netfilter subsystem (such as prerouting, input, forward, output, and postrouting) to dictate exactly when traffic should be evaluated. Rules & Expressions: The actual logic applied to packets. Rules are built using modular expressions to match packet data (e.g., IP addresses, ports) and statements to trigger actions (such as accept, drop, reject, or log). Unified Syntax: Replaces the fragmented commands of legacy tools with a single, streamlined command-line utility (nft) and a cleaner, more intuitive configuration syntax. Enhanced Performance: Uses advanced data structures like sets, dictionaries, and maps to achieve fast lookup times, significantly reducing CPU overhead when handling massive rule lists. Granular Logging & Security: Extensively deployed in enterprise environments and security labs to enforce strict access controls, mitigate network attacks, and generate verbose connection logs for traffic auditing. tags/rsyslog.html.title: rsyslog
tags/rsyslog.html.description: rsyslog (Rocket-fast system for log processing) is a high-performance, open-source utility for collecting, transforming, and forwarding log messages on UNIX and Linux systems. It extends the traditional syslog protocol with an advanced, modular architecture, allowing it to handle massive volumes of log data and route it securely to local files, databases, or centralized log management servers. Input Modules (im*): Responsible for gathering log messages from various sources. Examples include imuxsock (local Unix sockets), imklog (kernel messages), imudp (unreliable but fast network reception), and imtcp (reliable network log reception). Filtering Engine & RainerScript: A powerful, script-based configuration language (RainerScript) that allows administrators to filter, parse, and manipulate logs based on complex conditions, property matches, or regex patterns before they are sent to a destination. Output Modules (om*): Dictate where the processed logs are sent. Logs can be written to local files via omfile, forwarded over the network using omfwd, injected into databases via database modules, or piped into external scripts and security tools. Centralized Logging Architecture: Widely used to aggregate logs from dozens or thousands of network devices and servers into a single, hardened repository for easier monitoring and auditing. High Throughput & Multi-threading: Engineered for performance, it utilizes a heavily multi-threaded design and enterprise-grade buffering capabilities to prevent log loss, even during high-traffic network spikes or system resource exhaustion. Secure Log Transport: Supports enterprise-level security features, such as TLS encryption and mutual authentication, ensuring that sensitive log data is protected against tampering and eavesdropping while in transit. info_showOrphanNodes.description: Show nodes that are not connected to any other nodes.

info_showAttachments.description: Show attachments like images and PDFs as nodes in the graph.

info_allowGlobalGraph.description: Allow the user to view the global graph of all nodes.

info_allowExpand.description: Allow the user to pop-out the graph view to take up the whole screen

info_attractionForce.description: How much should linked nodes attract each other? This will make the graph appear more clustered.

info_linkLength.description: How long should the links between nodes be? The shorter the links the more connected nodes will cluster together.

info_repulsionForce.description: How much should nodes repel each other? This will make disconnected parts more spread out.

info_centralForce.description: How much should nodes be attracted to the center? This will make the graph appear more dense and circular.

info_edgePruning.description: Edges with a length above this threshold will not be rendered, however they will still contribute to the simulation. This can help large tangled graphs look more organised. Hovering over a node will still display these links.

info_minNodeRadius.description: How small should the smallest nodes be? The smaller a node is the less it will attract other nodes.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.

info_allowResizing.description: Whether or not to allow the sidebars to be resized

info_allowCollapsing.description: Whether or not to allow the sidebars to be collapsed

info_rightDefaultWidth.description: The default width of the right sidebar

info_leftDefaultWidth.description: The default width of the left sidebar
